text:
## Observations

1. Each undirected edge can be traversed in either direction, with the same label.
2. A path stays simple if each extension uses a vertex absent from the current path.
3. Appending an edge updates the running XOR by XORing it with that edge’s label, starting from zero.
4. Reaching vertex N completes a candidate path, and connectivity guarantees at least one candidate.
5. With at most ten vertices, all simple paths can be explored by backtracking.

## Solution sketch

> Each undirected edge can be traversed in either direction, with the same label.

1. Read the input and build a weighted adjacency list. For each edge, add an entry at each endpoint with the other endpoint and the edge label.

> A path stays simple if each extension uses a vertex absent from the current path.

2. Start a depth-first search at vertex 1 and mark it as visited. For each unvisited neighbor, mark it, recurse, then unmark it on return so other paths can use it. Every simple path from vertex 1 can be followed by these choices, and every explored prefix is simple.

> Appending an edge updates the running XOR by XORing it with that edge’s label, starting from zero.

3. Pass a running XOR into each recursive call. Start with zero and pass the current XOR combined with the chosen edge label to the next call. Each call keeps its own value, so backtracking only needs to restore the visited marks.

> Reaching vertex N completes a candidate path, and connectivity guarantees at least one candidate.

4. Initialize the best value to \(2^{60}\), which exceeds every possible path XOR. When a call reaches vertex \(N\), update the best value with the current XOR and return from that branch. Print the best value after the search. This also handles a direct edge from 1 to \(N\), a graph with only one possible path, and a minimum XOR of zero.

> With at most ten vertices, all simple paths can be explored by backtracking.

5. Each search call corresponds to an ordered prefix of distinct vertices after vertex 1. There are at most \(\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}(N-1)!/(N-1-k)!\) such prefixes, which is \(O((N-1)!)\). Scanning at most \(N-1\) neighbors per call gives an \(O(N(N-1)!)\) time bound. The adjacency list, visited marks, and recursion stack use \(O(N+M)\) space.

isolation.mechanism: codex exec, fresh ephemeral session, empty temporary working directory, user config and exec rules ignored, read-only sandbox, web search and listed features disabled, credential-like variables removed from the environment
isolation.limits: Codex harness instructions and its own tool descriptions remain in the model context; they cannot be removed. Tool isolation is verified post hoc from the event stream, which contained no tool, command, file or search events.
